proof_nl:
Let n>1 be an integer, and let t be a real number with (n-1)/n <= t < 1. Fix an integer k with 1 <= k <= n. We show that floor(k t) = k-1.

Since t < 1 and k > 0, we have k t < k.
Also,

k t >= k(n-1)/n = k - k/n.

Because k <= n, we have k/n <= 1, hence k - k/n >= k-1. Therefore

k-1 <= k t < k.

Now k-1 is an integer, and by the defining property of the floor function, if an integer m satisfies m <= y < m+1 then floor(y)=m. Applying this with y = k t and m = k-1 gives

floor(k t) = k-1.

Since k was arbitrary, the conclusion holds for every integer k with 1 <= k <= n.
solver_summary: Use the bounds (n-1)/n <= t < 1 to show k-1 <= kt < k for each 1<=k<=n, then apply the defining property of the floor function.
vetter_reason: The proof correctly shows that for any integer k with 1 <= k <= n and any t in [(n-1)/n, 1), one has k-1 <= k t < k, so floor(k t)=k-1. This exactly matches the lemma statement and the assembly role.
